title: Effect of Static vs. Conversational AI-Generated Messages on Colorectal Cancer Screening Intent: a Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) generated communication can more effectively increase intentions to undergo colorectal cancer (CRC) screening than standard educational material or no message at all. It directly compares a concise static AI-generated message with a more interactive AI chatbot conversation designed around motivational interviewing principles.

In a preregistered four-arm randomized controlled trial, 915 U.S. adults aged 45–75 who had never completed CRC screening were recruited online. Participants were assigned to one of four conditions: no-message control, a JAMA patient-page educational handout, a single GPT-4.1-generated personalized message, or a GPT-4.1 chatbot conversation personalized with demographic information and prompted to use motivational interviewing techniques. Everyone had to spend at least three minutes with their assigned material.

The primary outcomes were post-intervention self-reported 12-month intentions to complete colonoscopy and stool testing. Both AI conditions increased screening intentions relative to no message, but they did not outperform expert-written materials for colonoscopy intent. For stool-test intent, both AI conditions performed better than the expert materials, with the single-message AI and chatbot showing similar effects. The main conclusion is that brief, demographically tailored AI messages may be as persuasive as more complex chatbot conversations, and that AI may be especially useful for promoting less familiar, lower-burden screening options such as stool testing.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with a clear comparison arm structure, large sample size, and robust statistical analysis. It directly tests causal effects of LLM-generated interventions versus standard materials and no-message control, with credible implementation and reported effect sizes.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects are modest-to-medium on intentions, with the strongest effects on stool-test intent (d≈0.60-0.64) but not on colonoscopy intent relative to expert materials. The study is in a general adult population, not the target K-12 middle-school mathematics population, so practical educational relevance for the retrieval topic is very low despite the methodologically strong evidence.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4.1-generated persuasive messaging and a multi-turn motivational-interviewing chatbot used to encourage colorectal cancer screening intentions; both AI arms were personalized with participant demographics and compared against expert-written materials and no-message control.

finding.finding_summary: Both AI interventions increased self-reported comfort discussing colorectal cancer screening with a provider relative to no-message control and expert-written materials. The paper reports that participants found both AI conditions more empathetic than expert materials, but it does not provide a numeric effect size for this secondary outcome.
finding.measure: Self-reported comfort discussing CRC screening with a provider; perceived empathy of message/interaction

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the single AI message may be more scalable than the longer chatbot because it achieved similar intent gains with less participant time. Participants spent on average 180 seconds more with the chatbot than with the single AI message, yet the two AI formats did not differ in screening-intent effects.
finding.measure: Surplus time spent engaging with intervention
finding.std_deviation: Chatbot surplus time SD=260.46 sec; single AI message SD=69.61 sec; expert material SD=78.46 sec
